awd_titl_txt: NRI/Collaborative Research: Robotic Disassembly of High-Precision Electronic Devices
awd_abstract_narration:
The National Robotics Initiative (NRI) project addresses the increasing quantity of discarded high-precision electronics such as cell phones, tablets, and laptops. Current recycling methods rely on shredding after battery removal, due to high labor costs for disassembly. As a result, many valuable components are buried in landfills and not recycled. Disassembly, the first step of recycling, is more complex than assembly since there is much more variability in product type and, as a result, remanufacturing is usually not profitable. This award supports research to provide the fundamental understanding needed for the development of a novel robotic system that can effectively perform high-precision disassembly operations and make them practically and economically viable. The work has potential to mitigate labor shortages in recycling industry, reduce electronics waste, and revolutionize the remanufacturing of high-precision electronics. The research involves several disciplines including 3D sensing, deep learning, and robotics. The multidisciplinary research will be integrated into a series of educational and outreach activities which will increase the participation of underrepresented groups in research and positively impact engineering education.

Unlike the robotic assembly lines that assemble products, programming robots for repetitive operations is not a feasible solution for disassembly due to the widely varying types of discarded high-precision electronics. Therefore, disassembly of high-precision electronics is significantly more complex than assembly and requires high robotic adaptability, dexterity and accuracy. The research aims to enable a novel robotic system that can accurately see, interpret, and disassemble high-precision electronics through integrated and convergent research on 3D sensing, deep learning, robotic hand design, and high-precision manipulation. In particular, the research team will (1) perform accurate 3D sensing for complex surfaces exhibiting wide ranges of optical properties and reflectivity variations; (2) design and optimize the design of deep learning architectures for 3D point cloud interpretation; and (3) design a novel lightweight cable-driven robotic hand and develop a high-precision manipulation algorithm enabling efficient learning from experience.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project developed new technologies that enable robots to automatically perceive, interpret, and assist in the disassembly of complex electronic devices. As electronic waste continues to grow worldwide, recovering valuable materials from discarded electronics has become an increasingly important environmental and economic challenge. Electronic products contain valuable resources such as aluminum, copper, rare earth materials, and precious metals, yet many of these materials are lost because disassembly and recycling remain labor-intensive, costly, and difficult to automate. A major obstacle to automation is that robots often struggle to accurately perceive and understand complex electronic assemblies containing small components, reflective surfaces, hidden fasteners, and intricate structures. The goal of this project was to develop new technologies that enable robots to better "see," "understand," and ultimately help disassemble high-precision electronic devices.

To address these challenges, the project developed advanced sensing and perception technologies that allow robots to acquire detailed information about electronic products before manipulation. Researchers developed high-speed three-dimensional (3D) imaging systems capable of capturing accurate geometric information from complex electronic assemblies, including hard disk drives and computer components. Unlike conventional imaging systems, the developed technologies were designed to operate on objects with highly reflective, metallic, and high-contrast surfaces that often cause failures in traditional robotic vision systems. New optical sensing methods were created to improve measurement reliability and generate accurate 3D models of electronic devices under challenging real-world conditions.

The project also developed new artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques that enable robots to interpret complex scenes and identify critical components required for disassembly. These methods allow robots to recognize electronic components, locate screws and fasteners, identify device orientation, and generate detailed digital representations of assemblies. By combining high-resolution 3D imaging with intelligent scene understanding, the project established integrated robotic perception systems that provide both geometric and semantic information needed for robotic decision-making and manipulation. These capabilities represent an important step toward intelligent robotic disassembly systems that can adapt to variations in device designs and operating conditions.

Several technical advances emerged from the project. New high dynamic range 3D imaging methods were developed to improve measurement accuracy for reflective electronic components. Machine learning techniques were created to recover missing depth information when conventional optical measurements fail. Additional methods were developed to restore degraded imaging data and improve the robustness of 3D reconstruction under challenging lighting conditions. The project also explored secure optical sensing approaches that help protect sensitive measurement information. Collectively, these advances expanded the capabilities of robotic perception systems and contributed new knowledge to the fields of robotics, computer vision, optical metrology, and intelligent automation.

In addition to advances in robotic perception, the project developed a virtual reality (VR) training environment for human-robot collaborative disassembly. The VR platform enables users to safely learn, practice, and evaluate disassembly procedures within immersive virtual environments while interacting with simulated robotic systems. This capability allows operators to gain experience before working with physical equipment and provides a cost-effective approach for workforce training. The platform also supports the generation of synthetic data that can be used to improve robotic motion planning, task execution, and autonomous decision-making. By creating a bridge between human learning and robotic learning, the VR environment extends the impact of the project beyond robotic hardware and sensing technologies.

The project produced broader impacts in sustainability, manufacturing, and workforce development. By enabling greater automation of electronic waste processing, the technologies developed through this research may help increase recovery of valuable materials, reduce waste sent to landfills, and improve the efficiency of recycling and remanufacturing operations. More effective recovery and reuse of materials can contribute to resource conservation, reduced environmental impacts, and support for a circular economy. The technologies may also benefit other application areas that require accurate 3D sensing and intelligent automation, including advanced manufacturing, quality inspection, infrastructure monitoring, and industrial maintenance.

The project also contributed to the education and training of future scientists and engineers. Graduate students received hands-on experience in robotics, artificial intelligence, computer vision, optical metrology, virtual reality, software development, and advanced sensing technologies. Through participation in interdisciplinary research activities, students developed technical, analytical, and professional skills while contributing to peer-reviewed publications and technical presentations. These experiences helped prepare students for careers in academia, industry, and government laboratories.

Overall, this project established new foundations for intelligent robotic disassembly by advancing the integration of robotics, artificial intelligence, 3D sensing, and immersive training technologies. The outcomes demonstrate how innovations in perception, automation, and human-robot collaboration can help address important societal challenges related to electronic waste, resource recovery, sustainability, and workforce development. The knowledge, technologies, and trained personnel resulting from this project are expected to support future advances in intelligent automation and sustainable manufacturing for years to come.

  • Results of the vision system. For both sides of a hard drive, the system identifies key components, builds a 3D model, and automatically labels each part. Because both steps use the same camera view, no extra alignment is needed.
    Reproduced from Balasubramaniam, B., Suresh, V., Metcalf, B., and Li, B., Fringe Projection Based Vision Pipeline for Autonomous Hard Drive Disassembly, arXiv:2604.17231, 2026.
    Public Domain
    Beiwen Li
    Vision Pipeline for Robotic Disassembly of Hard Disk Devices
  • Demonstration of human-robot teamwork for hard drive disassembly. The robot and human safely work together to remove and sort components. The robot avoids human hands, assists with handling parts, provides error alerts, and completes the task.
    Reproduced from Li, B.; Zheng, M.; Liang, X.; et al., Machines, 2025, 13, 239.
    Creative Commons
    Beiwen Li
    VR training for human-robot collaborative hard disk disassembly
  • Comparison of the full MMDC-Net (top row) and simplified versions. Columns show the reference 3D shape, reconstructed shape, predicted missing regions, true missing regions, and error maps. Results highlight the importance of each design component for accurate 3D recovery.
